profiles.name: Peter Brown
profiles.description: Peter Brown was a U.S. Army officer and West Point graduate who applied for conscientious-objector recognition while serving in Iraq. After the Army denied his application, he brought a federal habeas petition. According to his civil-liberties lawyers, the Army reconsidered and approved his application on August 28, 2007. His case involved religious opposition to military service and a successful administrative reconsideration, rather than a prison sentence.
profiles.query: "Peter Brown" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: NYCLU confirms the West Point officer's conscientious-objector discharge. Reject Revolutionary/World War soldiers, historian, Australian objector and Peter Sean Brown ICE-case portraits as namesakes.

profiles.name: Ronnie Tallman
profiles.description: Ronnie Tallman is a Navajo Marine who enlisted in October 2004 and later became a hand-trembler, a traditional Diné healer whose obligations conflicted with harming others. He went on unauthorized absence rather than deploy to Iraq, then applied for conscientious-objector status in January 2006. After an initial denial, the Marine Corps granted the application in January 2007. The available record documents an administrative process, not an arrest, court-martial or confinement.
profiles.query: "Ronnie Tallman" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Indianz January 2007 story identifies Navajo Marine and includes an image lead; verification pending.

profiles.name: Matthis Chiroux
profiles.description: Matthis Chiroux was an Army veteran who refused a 2008 recall from the Individual Ready Reserve for deployment to Iraq. He argued publicly that participation would violate his conscience. An administrative separation board heard his case on April 21, 2009. In his account afterward, he described receiving a general discharge under honorable conditions from the reserve, while retaining the benefits attached to his earlier honorable discharge from active duty. The administrative misconduct finding was not a criminal conviction or prison sentence.
profiles.query: "Matthis Chiroux" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Named Platon portrait in Huffington Post and documentary stills are leads requiring image and rights review.

profiles.name: Chris Capps
profiles.description: Chris Capps was an Army communications specialist from New Jersey who served in Baghdad from November 2005 to September 2006. He went absent without leave from his unit in Germany in March 2007 rather than deploy to Afghanistan, surrendered at Fort Sill on May 8, and received an other-than-honorable administrative discharge on May 11. Available firsthand and contemporaneous accounts do not document a court-martial, jail booking or confinement during that three-day out-processing period.
profiles.query: "Chris Capps" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Stars and Stripes identifies 440th unit soldier; Courage to Resist index is a portrait lead, host previously inaccessible.

profiles.name: Eugene Cherry
profiles.description: Eugene Cherry was an Army medic and Iraq veteran who went absent without leave to obtain treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder. After he returned to Fort Drum, the Army prepared to court-martial him. With support from counselors, lawyers, and antiwar veterans, he challenged that response. In July 2007, the Army abandoned the court-martial and gave him a general discharge under honorable conditions, without a prison sentence or reduction in rank. His case involved access to care after combat.
profiles.query: "Eugene Cherry" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist index identifies medic; IMDb result alone does not verify identity. Portrait lead pending host access.

profiles.name: Clifton Hicks
profiles.description: Clifton Hicks served in Iraq as a U.S. Army soldier before becoming a conscientious objector. In recorded interviews, he described how his wartime experiences changed his beliefs and led him to oppose continued military service. He obtained conscientious-objector recognition and later spoke publicly about the war. The sources used for this profile do not establish a prison sentence.
profiles.query: "Clifton Hicks" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: TPR/PBS American Veteran identifies Iraq veteran; TPR web fetch failed. Reject WWII Clifton Hicks photo at UNT as namesake.

profiles.name: Hart Viges
profiles.description: Benjamin Hart Viges served in Iraq with the Army’s 82nd Airborne Division after enlisting on September 12, 2001. His experience during house raids and combat led him to seek conscientious-objector status on Christian grounds. After a ten-month application process, the Army approved his claim and honorably discharged him in 2004. He later worked with Iraq Veterans Against the War, the GI Rights Hotline and youth counter-recruitment programs. His discharge involved no arrest or imprisonment.
profiles.query: "Hart Viges" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Official Texas oral history confirms identity but image URL is unavailable.jpg, a placeholder. Rag Blog and veterans publications remain photo leads.

profiles.name: Carl Webb
profiles.description: Carl Webb was a U.S. military veteran who refused Iraq service after his term was extended. In a recorded interview, he described leaving the military rather than take part in a war he opposed. His resistance became part of the public campaign against involuntary extensions of military service. The sources used here establish his refusal and antiwar position, but not a criminal conviction or prison sentence.
profiles.query: "Carl Webb" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: PRX interview verifies resister; Flickr Portraits of Courage is paintings, not real portrait. Reject rugby player and Somerton Man namesakes.

profiles.name: Phil McDowell
profiles.description: Phil McDowell was a U.S. Army sergeant who served in Iraq from March 2004 to March 2005. After completing active service and receiving a discharge in June 2006, the Army recalled him for another Iraq deployment under the stop-loss program. He went to Canada in October 2006 and sought permission to remain as a war resister. Available records document immigration litigation and threatened military prosecution, but no arrest, court-martial or imprisonment.
profiles.query: "Phil McDowell" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: GQ Just Desert is a strong identity-specific reporting lead; photo review pending.

profiles.name: Rodney Watson
profiles.description: Rodney Watson is a U.S. Army Iraq veteran from Kansas City who went to Canada in 2006 after refusing continued service under stop-loss orders. When Canadian authorities ordered his removal, he entered sanctuary at Vancouver’s First United Church on September 18, 2009. He remained within the church for years to avoid arrest and deportation while pursuing immigration relief. Church sanctuary severely restricted his movement but was not jail or prison confinement, and no U.S. criminal custody is documented.
profiles.query: "Rodney Watson" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Georgia Straight and Vice have identity-specific photo leads; Dartmouth/Justseeds images are artwork, not photographs.

profiles.name: Chuck Wiley
profiles.description: Chuck Wiley is a former Navy chief petty officer and nuclear engineer from Kentucky who served about 16 years in the U.S. military. While assigned to the USS Enterprise in 2006, he concluded that the Iraq War was unlawful and morally wrong. He left the Navy and moved to Canada in 2007 rather than continue participating. Canadian proceedings concerned his immigration status; available records do not document a U.S. arrest, court-martial or confinement.
profiles.query: "Chuck Wiley" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Verified Matthew Hill photo in In These Times; deployed and browser-checked with undistorted 3:2 appearance.

profiles.name: Benjamin Lewis
profiles.description: Benjamin Lewis, known as Benji Lewis, was a Marine who served two tours in Iraq and later refused recall through the Individual Ready Reserve. His account appeared in the military-resister oral-history collection About Face. A review of that collection reports that his refusal ended in discharge without penalties. This profile concerns his military resistance and does not assert a prison sentence.
profiles.query: "Benjamin Lewis" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Reprinted bar photograph identifies Benjamin Lewis/Benji Lewis; original reporting/credit must be traced. Reject Civil War and Revolutionary War namesakes.

profiles.name: Dean Walcott
profiles.description: Dean Walcott was a U.S. Marine Iraq veteran who sought refuge in Canada. His case was discussed in Canada's House of Commons in 2008, where speakers described how service during the invasion and later contact with wounded soldiers contributed to his decision to leave the military. This historical refuge profile does not establish a prison sentence or his present immigration status.
profiles.query: "Dean Walcott" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Amnesty and Le Parisien identify Marine Dean William Walcott; photo lead pending verification.

profiles.name: James Circello
profiles.description: James Circello was an Army airborne infantry sergeant who served in northern Iraq from March 2003 to March 2004. He left his unit in Vicenza, Italy on April 10, 2007 rather than deploy to Afghanistan. After months of public anti-war activity, he surrendered at Fort Knox in November 2007 and was administratively discharged within three days. Contemporary reporting states that he was released from the Army instead of imprisoned and does not document jail or stockade confinement.
profiles.query: "James Circello" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist and VVAW identify airborne infantry war resister; image lead pending verification.

profiles.name: Chas Davis
profiles.description: Chas Davis was a U.S. Army military policeman who applied for conscientious-objector status in 2004 while stationed in South Korea. After review of his application, the Army honorably discharged him in January 2005. He later advised other service members seeking conscientious-objector recognition. The administrative proceeding involved no documented arrest, court-martial or imprisonment.
profiles.query: "Chas Davis" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist describes Army MP in Korea. Reject track-and-field coach and historical admiral namesakes.

profiles.name: Diedra Cobb
profiles.description: Diedra Cobb was a U.S. Army intelligence specialist who sought conscientious-objector status in 2003 and told her superiors that she would not fire a weapon in Iraq. Courage to Resist reports that her application was denied, but she was transferred to the Individual Ready Reserve and did not deploy to Iraq. No prison sentence is established.
profiles.query: "Diedra Cobb" war conscientious objector portrait photo
profiles.finding: VVAW firsthand article and WRL award sources identify objector; photo/credit verification pending.

profiles.name: Elga Mari Castro Ramos
profiles.description: Elga Mari Castro Ramos was arrested during the 2000 civil-disobedience campaign against U.S. Navy training on Vieques, Puerto Rico. The First Circuit identifies this person among defendants arrested between April and June 2000 after entering Camp García to oppose the exercises and their effects on residents and the environment. Following a nonjury trial, the defendant was convicted under 18 U.S.C. § 1382. The consolidated appeal, United States v. Sued-Jiménez, upheld the convictions on December 19, 2001. The opinion does not specify this defendant’s sentence or the length of physical confinement.
profiles.query: "Elga Mari Castro Ramos" Vieques foto
profiles.finding: First Circuit opinion confirms identity; no verified portrait found.
